latest_final:
| The speaker of the repeated sentence is a person breaking off a relationship for good—but the "I" who says "You've disappointed me so much; I'm never coming back" is not the person physically writing the words out. Someone copied that invented farewell seven times in imitation of another person's handwriting: deliberate rehearsal at forging that person's script. That rehearsal is preparation for a false farewell note—a note meant to make it appear that the other spouse simply walked out of the marriage, deliberately and forever.

What sits behind the forgery is a death: the spouse whose handwriting is being imitated has been killed, and the killer is the person who benefits from the story that the victim voluntarily left. The rehearsed practice writing and the intended forged "I'm never coming back" note are in one and the same hand—the forger's, not the victim's; the words themselves are the forger's own invention, put into the dead spouse's mouth.

The final line, "Sigh, I know I'm in trouble," belongs to the forger, and it is anticipatory: it comes as the rehearsal is finished, before any discovery or arrest, when the forger already recognizes the legal consequences that must eventually follow from the murder and the forged farewell. So the repeated line is the murdered spouse's fabricated voice, while the sighing "I" is the killer-forger dreading what they know is coming.
